# Self-study: Reporting from your repository {.unnumbered} Two tasks finish the record your workshop repository has built up during the day: a check that every result in a report is computed rather than typed, then a README drafted from the files you made. Both split the work the same way: you own the facts, the AI writes the text around them, and an independent check, not the AI, tells you whether to trust it. *Self-study: about 25 minutes, after the workshop day.* **Start state:** your workshop repository on `main`, with your work from the day committed. If Block 7 is unfinished, switch to the `checkpoint-cleaning` branch from the Git pane's branch menu **first**, and do the whole page there. :::{#reporting-files .callout-note collapse="true"} ## This page's files, and how it fits You work in the **same workshop repository**, with the `AGENTS.md` from Block 4 and the deny rules from Block 5, and check the agent's work from the R console and the Git pane, as in [checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work). Part A scans a report that ships with the template. Part B's README draws on two files you made during the day: your AI-use log (Block 3) and your codebook (Block 7). If Block 7 is unfinished, the `checkpoint-cleaning` branch has both. Either way, every file you need is in the repository; nothing needs downloading. Two more statistical checks (robustness and simulation) are in *Going further*. How the two tasks split the work: | You own | The AI writes | The independent check | |---|---|---| | The numbers in your report | Text around inline code | Is any number typed rather than computed? | | The codebook, scripts, tests, lockfile and AI-use log | A README drafted from them | Can every statement be traced to one of those files? | **Shipped with the template.** You run or read these; you do not create them. | File | Its job | Used in | |---|---|---| | `scripts/functions/typed_numbers.R` | Lists prose lines with numbers outside inline code | Part A | | `reports/example_report.qmd` | An interim report with some results typed in | Part A | | `tests/test_readme.R` | Checks the README against the files it was drafted from | Part B | **Created in an earlier block.** | File | Created by | Used in | |---|---|---| | `docs/ai-log.md` | You, Block 3 (a line per block since) | Part B: the README's AI declaration | | `docs/codebook.csv` | You, Block 7, from the agent's draft | Part B: the README's data dictionary | **Created on this page.** | File | Created by | Step | |---|---|---| | `README.md` | The agent | Part B, step 1 | | A new line in `docs/ai-log.md` | You | Part B, step 3 | ::: ## Part A: Reporting without typed numbers :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Scan a report :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** find the results in a report that were typed rather than computed, so that each can become inline code that updates when the data change. **Start state:** the template's `reports/example_report.qmd`, an interim summary of the voles trial with some numbers typed in. **1. Scan it.** In the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "typed_numbers.R")) find_typed_numbers(here::here("reports", "example_report.qmd")) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf) ``` ::: **2. Sort the hits.** The scan flags five lines. Decide for each one whether it is a typed result that should be inline code, or a number that is fine as text.
Lines 37 and 38 are typed results (the 1.53 g difference with its interval, and the mean of 29.4 g): both should be inline code. The other three can stay: the date in the YAML header (line 3), the design size of 12 per arm-by-sex combination (line 28), and "95%" in "95% CI" (line 34).
**You are done when** you can say which two lines are typed results and why the other three can stay. **If it goes wrong:** if `find_typed_numbers()` is not found, check that the `source()` line ran without an error. :::: ::: The same scan works on any `.qmd` you write, including your Quarto report from Day 3. Every hit is a question, not an error. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How it works: inline code, and what the scan checks A typed number can be mistyped, or go stale when the data change, and an assistant drafting text may restate numbers it saw earlier. So every number in the prose comes from inline code: a code chunk computes the result, and the text calls it with `` `r round(primary$estimate, 2)` ``. `reports/example_report.qmd`, the report you scanned, does this in the first paragraph of its Results. Your `AGENTS.md` asks for this; the shipped `find_typed_numbers()` checks it, by listing prose lines that still contain numbers outside inline code. ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `scripts/functions/typed_numbers.R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/typed_numbers.R ---- # List the prose lines of a .qmd file that still contain numbers outside # inline code, for you to review by eye. Years, design sizes and YAML values # are flagged too, so treat each hit as a question, not an error. find_typed_numbers <- function(path) { lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE) is_fence <- grepl("^```", lines) in_chunk <- cumsum(is_fence) %% 2 == 1 tibble::tibble(line = seq_along(lines), text = lines) |> dplyr::filter(!in_chunk, !is_fence) |> dplyr::mutate(prose = gsub("`\\{?r\\}? [^`]*`", "", text)) |> dplyr::filter(grepl("[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+|\\b[0-9]{2,}\\b", prose, perl = TRUE)) |> dplyr::select(line, text) } ``` ::: ::: ## Part B: A README from the record Your repository now holds most of what a reader needs: a codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI., cleaning logs, numbered scripts, a lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., tests and an AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.. A README pulls them together. The rule: the AI may only phrase facts you can trace to a file; anything else becomes a visible placeholder for you to fill. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Draft from the record, then test it :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** a README drafted only from your repository's files and checked against them by a test, so that a reader can trace every statement in it to a source. **Start state:** your workshop repository on `main` (or `checkpoint-cleaning`), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode in the Terminal tab. **1. Draft.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Draft README.md from these files only, naming the source of each section: - Data dictionary, as a Markdown table whose first column is the column name: docs/codebook.csv - Scripts and run order: the numbered scripts in scripts/ - Dependencies: the R version in renv.lock, and renv::restore() - How to verify, from a terminal: Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')", and what the tests in tests/ check - AI declaration: docs/ai-log.md, claiming nothing beyond it Anything these files do not give (authors, licence, DOI, a unit the codebook leaves blank or as ) becomes a placeholder in exactly this form: **TODO: supply [field]: not provided** Edit README.md only. ``` Approve the edit when asked, after reading it. **Answer each request with plain Yes or No.** Never choose an option that says *don't ask again*: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. **2. Let the tests audit it.** Restart R (*Session → Restart R*), then in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests")) ``` ::: The shipped `tests/test_readme.R` checks the README against the files it was drafted from, and reports how many placeholders are left; *How it works*, after this task, lists what it checks. **3. Check the scope, log it and commit.** The Git pane should show only `README.md` as changed. Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md`, for example: ``` 2026-10-20; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); drafted README.md from the repository's files; kept the draft after test_readme.R passed, placeholders still to fill ``` Then commit `README.md` and the log from the Git pane. **You are done when** `test_readme.R` passes, the agent changed only `README.md`, and the README and your log line are committed. **If it goes wrong:** if the agent changed any file other than `README.md`, select it in the Git pane and choose **Revert**. If the README test fails, ask Claude Code to fix only the statements the test names, and run the suite again. :::: ::: **Ask yourself:** what did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again? :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How it works: the README's sources, and what the test checks ::::::: {.dia .dia-flow role="figure" aria-label="The README is drafted by the AI only from five kinds of file in your repository, the only sources: docs/codebook.csv, the numbered scripts in scripts/, the tests in tests/, renv.lock and docs/ai-log.md. The AI drafts README.md, with placeholders for anything missing. You trace every statement to a file."} :::::: {.dia-branches} ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `docs/codebook.csv` ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} numbered scripts in `scripts/` ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} tests in `tests/` ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `renv.lock` ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `docs/ai-log.md` ::: :::::: ::: {.dia-arrow} the only sources ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Drafts `README.md`, with placeholders for anything missing ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} You trace every statement to a file ::: ::::::: The shipped `tests/test_readme.R` checks the R version in `renv.lock` and the `renv::restore()` command, every numbered script, no leftover `{{` tokens, and no invented unit in the data-dictionary table row for a column the codebook leaves without a unit: that row must hold a TODO instead. It also reports how many placeholders are left. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using another tool Posit Assistant can do Part B with the same prompt. Use it in Normal mode, so it asks before each change. The checks do not change: the test suite in a fresh R session, and the Git pane. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Stretch: audit the README by hand The test checks the R version, the scripts, leftover tokens and blank units. Trace the statements it cannot check yourself: confirm that the AI declarationA statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded. says no more than your log, and that each section names a source you gave it. **Before you share it,** the placeholders are your to-do list. Work through licence, ORCIDs, DOI and archiving with the [SORTEE checklist from Day 2](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-sortee), then commit. A fuller version, with a README skill, is in *Going further* on the self-study page on [AI-assisted code review](11h-code-review.qmd). ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** find the results in a report that were typed rather than computed, and have an agent draft a README, **trusted because** a scan lists every number outside inline code, a shipped test checks the README against its sources, and the whole suite passes in a fresh R session. - **Check:** a scan for typed numbers; every README statement traced to a file. - **Reproduce:** numbers come from code, so the report updates when the data do; the README's dependencies come from `renv.lock`, not from memory. - **Record:** the README and the AI-use log complete the record. Together with the codebook, logs, tests and lockfile, they are what a reviewer, a co-author or you in a year's time will need. Check your institution's and target journal's policy on declaring AI use. ::: ## Check your understanding **`find_typed_numbers()` lists a line of your report. What does that tell you?**
**The README draft gives the unit of `metabolic_rate_post`, but your codebook leaves it blank. What should you do?**
## Going further This material is optional. Work through it if it is useful to you. :::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Robustness, not choice AI should not choose your primary analysis. The BLADE benchmark compared language-model agents with expert analysts on open-ended research questions. It found that the models were often limited to basic analyses, and that agents able to explore the data made more varied but still sub-optimal analytical decisions (Gu et al., 2024). Its useful role is narrower: listing defensible alternatives to an analysis you have already fixed, so you can check whether your conclusion depends on the choice. Run the steps yourself, and judge each answer before running it. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Enumerate, judge, run :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** run defensible alternatives beside your fixed primary analysis, so that you know whether your conclusion depends on the analysis choice, without letting the AI make that choice. **1. Ask for alternatives, not a recommendation:** ``` My pre-registered primary analysis is an ANCOVA: mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, estimating the High_dose versus Control difference. List alternative specifications a reasonable analyst might use for the same question, and for each, say whether it estimates the same quantity. Do not recommend one. ``` **2. Judge each one yourself.** Mark each alternative defensible or not, with a reason. Check especially whether it estimates the *same* quantity. **3. Run the defensible ones** and report them beside the primary analysis. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) voles_df <- load_voles() |> mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"))) specs_df <- tribble( ~spec, ~formula, "Primary: ANCOVA", "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex", "Change score", "I(mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) ~ treatment_arm + sex", "ANCOVA with arm-by-sex", "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm * sex" ) spec_results_df <- specs_df |> mutate(result = map(formula, \(f) { fit <- lm(as.formula(f), data = voles_df) ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble( estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) })) |> unnest(result) spec_results_df ``` :::
In the third specification, the coefficient `treatment_armHigh_dose` is the High_dose effect **in females only** (the reference level of `sex`), because the model includes an interaction. It sits in the same column as the other estimates but answers a different question. It belongs in a separate analysis of whether the effect differs by sex, not in a table of estimates of the same quantity. An AI that lists it as an "alternative" without saying so has made exactly the error step 2 asks you to catch.
**4. Log it.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` in the same form as in Part B: the tool and model, the alternatives it listed, and which you kept as defensible. **You are done when** every alternative is marked defensible or not, with a reason, and the table beside your primary estimate holds only specifications that estimate the same quantity. :::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} Running many specifications and reporting the one you like best is selective reporting. The primary analysis is fixed in advance; the others are reported as sensitivity analyses whatever they show. ::: #### Check your understanding: robustness **Why should the arm-by-sex interaction model not appear in the same robustness table as the primary ANCOVA?**
::::: :::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Simulation and parameter recovery If you simulate data from a mechanism whose parameters you chose, a correct analysis should recover those parameters on average, and its 95% confidence intervals should contain the true values about 95% of the time. This tests the analysis code against a known answer, which real data never provide. Morris, White and Crowther (2019) give a structure for planning simulation studies: the **aims**, the **data-generating mechanism**, the **estimand**, the **methods** and the **performance measures** (ADEMP). Here: - **Aim:** check that the analysis code estimates the high-dose effect correctly. - **Data-generating mechanism:** 12 voles per arm-by-sex cell. Pre-treatment mass is normal with mean 28 g and SD 2 g. Post-treatment mass equals 2.8 g plus 0.9 times pre-treatment mass, plus 0.8 g for Low_dose, plus 1.5 g for High_dose, plus 1.0 g for males, plus normal error with SD 0.8 g. - **Estimand:** the difference in post-treatment mass between High_dose and Control, adjusted for pre-treatment mass and sex. True value: 1.5 g. - **Method:** linear model (ANCOVA), `mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex`. - **Performance measures:** bias and confidence-interval coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error. The written mechanism is yours. It is the equivalent of the codebook in [Block 7](11g-data-cleaning.qmd): the AI turns it into code, and you check the code against it. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Write, check, recover :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** run your analysis code on data simulated from a mechanism you wrote, so that you test it against a known answer, which real data never give. **1. Simulation code.** Give the AI the data-generating mechanism above, word for word, and ask for a function `simulate_voles()` returning a tibble with columns `treatment_arm`, `sex`, `mass_pre_g` and `mass_post_g`. **2. Check the simulated data against the specification.** Before using the function, run it once and check that it matches what you wrote: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) sim_df <- simulate_voles() sim_df |> count(treatment_arm, sex) # 12 per cell? sim_df |> summarise(mean(mass_pre_g), sd(mass_pre_g)) sim_df |> summarise(mean_post = mean(mass_post_g), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex)) ``` ::: High_dose should be about 1.5 g above Control within each sex, and males about 1 g above females. If not, the simulation is wrong, and nothing built on it can be trusted. **3. Analysis code, in a separate session.** Without showing it the simulation code, ask the AI for a function `estimate_high_vs_control(data)` that fits the model above and returns the High_dose estimate and its 95% confidence interval. **4. Run the recovery.**
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} simulate_voles <- function(n_per_cell = 12, effect_low = 0.8, effect_high = 1.5, sex_effect = 1.0, slope_pre = 0.9, sd_pre = 2, sd_resid = 0.8) { tidyr::expand_grid( treatment_arm = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"), sex = c("F", "M"), animal = seq_len(n_per_cell) ) |> dplyr::mutate( mass_pre_g = stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), mean = 28, sd = sd_pre), arm_effect = dplyr::case_when( treatment_arm == "Low_dose" ~ effect_low, treatment_arm == "High_dose" ~ effect_high, .default = 0 ), mass_post_g = 28 * (1 - slope_pre) + slope_pre * mass_pre_g + arm_effect + sex_effect * (sex == "M") + stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), sd = sd_resid) ) |> dplyr::select(treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g) } estimate_high_vs_control <- function(data) { data <- dplyr::mutate( data, treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")) ) fit <- stats::lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = data) ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble::tibble( estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) } ``` :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) n_sim <- 1000 true_effect <- 1.5 results_df <- seq_len(n_sim) |> map(\(i) estimate_high_vs_control(simulate_voles(effect_high = true_effect))) |> list_rbind() results_df |> summarise( bias = mean(estimate) - true_effect, bias_mcse = sd(estimate) / sqrt(n_sim), coverage = mean(lower <= true_effect & upper >= true_effect), coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim), empirical_se = sd(estimate) ) ``` ::: Bias should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero. Coverage should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.95, roughly 0.936 to 0.964 with 1,000 runs. **5. Prove the check can fail.** Replace the analysis with a version that models the change the wrong way round, as in [Block 2](11c-debugging.qmd): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_buggy <- function(data) { data <- dplyr::mutate( data, treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")), mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g ) fit <- stats::lm(mass_change_g ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = data) ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble::tibble( estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) } ``` ::: Rerun the recovery with `estimate_buggy()`. Bias should be about −3 g and coverage near zero. A check you have never seen fail is a check you are assuming works. **6. Log it.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` in the same form as in Part B: the tool and model, the two functions it wrote, and what the recovery check showed. **You are done when** `estimate_high_vs_control()` gives bias and coverage within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of their targets, and `estimate_buggy()` fails the same check. :::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} **What recovery does not prove.** It shows that the code estimates the right quantity *under the mechanism you simulated*. It says nothing about whether real voles behave like that. A change-score model fitted to these simulated data would also be nearly unbiased (randomisation makes both estimators valid), but less precise; compare `empirical_se` to see the cost. Recovery tests code, not scientific assumptions. ::: #### Check your understanding: simulation **A simulation recovers the true effect with negligible bias and 95% coverage. What has it shown?**
::::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Translating from SPSS, Stata or SAS **Translation with an equivalence check** was the task your own agent did in [Block 6](11k-build-an-agent.qmd): `tests/test_translation.R` compared its tidyverse translation with the original base R code, run side by side in R. [Block 8](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd) explains why "the same as the original" is not the same as "correct". From other software, export the original's results to a file and compare the translation against those. Expect differences in defaults (missing values, quantiles, rounding); each needs a decision, not a looser tolerance. ::: ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
AI-use log A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.
AI declaration A statement, for example in a README, recording that an AI assisted, naming the tool, model and date, and making no claim about AI use beyond what was recorded.
codebook A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
````` ::: ::: ## References - Gu, K., Shang, R., Jiang, R., et al. (2024). BLADE: Benchmarking language model agents for data-driven science. In *Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024*, 13936–13971. - Morris, T.P., White, I.R. and Crowther, M.J. (2019).
